How Verse streams a 3-million-triangle building into your browser in seconds#

Open a link, and a whole apartment appears in your browser a few seconds later. No app, no download, no "please wait while we load hundreds of megabytes". That is what Verse Engine does, and this post explains how — in plain language, with pictures, for anyone who has ever waited for a 3D file to open.

The problem: 3D files are enormous, and browsers are not built for them#

A real building, scanned or modelled properly, is big. The flagship interior in our demos has about 3 million triangles and hundreds of photo-real textures. A phone scan of a single room can be ten times that. On disk such a scene is hundreds of megabytes to a few gigabytes.

The usual ways to show it all have the same flaw: someone has to download the whole thing before they see anything.

  • A video is small, but it is not the building — you cannot look where the camera did not go.
  • A viewer app can handle the file, but now your client has to install software, and their phone probably cannot hold the scene in memory anyway.
  • A web page can embed a 3D model, but web 3D expects small models. Drop a scanned building into it and the page freezes, then crashes.

The wait is not a bandwidth problem that faster internet will fix. Even on a fast connection, a phone cannot hold a building's worth of geometry and textures in memory at once. The whole-file approach is a dead end.

The idea: compile once, then send only what you look at#

Verse borrows the trick that made streaming video possible. A film is not sent to you as one file; it is prepared once into chunks of different quality, and your player fetches the next few seconds at the quality your connection can take. Verse does the same for space instead of time.

Step 1 — compile. When you upload a model, Verse does not shrink it. It compiles it, once, into a format built for streaming. The scene is cut into thousands of small pieces, and each piece is prepared at several levels of detail — from a rough version that costs almost nothing to the original, full-detail version. Textures are converted into the compact form graphics chips read directly, and sorted by how much of the scene they cover. The result is a single compiled file, cryptographically signed so that a viewer can prove it has not been tampered with.

Step 2 — stream what the camera sees. When someone opens the link, the viewer first fetches a few megabytes: the "table of contents" and the roughest level of every piece. That is enough to draw the whole building as a soft clay model, in the right colours, within a few seconds. Then, every frame, the viewer works out which pieces are in front of the camera, how big they appear on this screen, and asks the server for exactly those pieces at exactly the detail that would look sharp — nothing behind you, nothing too far away to matter. As you move, it fetches more and lets go of what you left behind.

Two consequences follow, and they are the whole point:

  1. The size of the scene stops mattering. A 30-million-triangle scan and a single chair cost the viewer about the same per frame, because the viewer only ever holds what it is looking at. Our measurements table shows both above 100 frames per second on the same laptop.
  2. The first seconds are the good seconds. Because the roughest level of everything arrives first, you see the whole space immediately and watch it sharpen, rather than staring at a progress bar and then getting everything at once.

The viewer also does something else quietly: it never does the heavy lifting on the page itself. The engine runs in a background thread of the browser, written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly, so the page you are on stays responsive even while the heaviest scene streams in.

The proof: measured, not eyeballed#

It is easy to make a 3D viewer that is fast by making it ugly, or beautiful by making it slow. Verse is checked against ground truth on both counts, automatically, and the numbers below come straight from the test harnesses in the repository, last re-run on 2 October 2026 on an Apple M5 Pro laptop in Chromium. No phone has been through the harness yet, so there are no phone numbers here.

What we measureResultWhere it comes from
Frame rate on a 30-million-triangle scanover 100 fps on a laptop (101–118 measured)docs/metrics-wall.md
Frame rate on the 3-million-triangle apartment120 fps on the same laptopdocs/metrics-wall.md
Time to first picture, the apartmentabout 4 s over the internet from the production server; under 1 s from a server on the same networkdocs/metrics-wall.md
Colour accuracy of baked architectural scenes vs the source bakemean colour error ΔE 0.6–2.5 on our apartment scenes (gate: below 6)web/test/fidelity.mjs
Colour accuracy of lit scenes vs a Blender reference renderΔE 0.5–8.2 on ten of eleven reference views (gate: below 9); one metal-helmet view is at 12 and is open workweb/test/fidelity-lit.mjs
Each renderer vs its own approved images0.000 % pixel difference on the golden image suite, 4 of 4web/test/golden.mjs

A word on that ΔE number: it is a standard measure of how different two colours look to a human eye. A ΔE of 1 is about the smallest difference a trained eye can see side by side; a ΔE of 5 is noticeable but still "the same colour" to most people. A baked interior — where the designer's lighting is already in the textures — lands under 3, which means what you see in Verse is what the designer saw in Blender. Scenes lit live by the engine are compared with a reference renderer, a different piece of software with its own lighting model, and sit higher.

What is new in 2.0#

Version 2.0 is the first production release, and most of what this post describes shipped in it. In everyday terms:

  • A link is the product. Upload once; share a URL that opens in current browsers, on laptops and phones. Make it private and hand out per-person access you can revoke later.
  • Clients can comment in the space. Anyone with the link can click a spot and leave a note pinned to that exact position — no account needed. You resolve or delete pins from the same link.
  • Video, without a render farm. One click records a flythrough of the scene to an MP4 or WebM in the viewer's own browser. Nothing is uploaded.
  • Embed it anywhere with one line. A single script tag puts the viewer on your own site, with events your page can listen to.
  • Publish from the tools you already use. Blender has a one-click "Publish to Verse" button; Unity and Unreal exporters are in early-access beta and not yet verified in the real editors. (Update, 4.0: the Unity and Unreal plug-ins have since been verified in the real editors — Unity 6000.6.5f1 and Unreal Engine 5.8.3 — and are no longer beta.)
  • It looks right. Physically based materials, reflections, HDR output on screens that support it, and a dedicated full-resolution path for the handful of surfaces in a scene that deserve it.
  • Compiles are faster. The 2.0.1 update made large-scene compiles about 1.8× faster with identical output (the flagship interior went from 15.9 to 8.8 minutes on our development laptop; on the hosted server it takes about 20).

The full list, with the engineering detail, is in the changelog; the human version is in the companion post, 2.0 release notes for humans.

What is next#

Three things are at the top of the list.

  • Shorter time-to-sharp for far-away viewers. Streaming is a chain of small requests, so distance to the server matters more than bandwidth. An edge cache close to the viewer roughly halves the time until a scene is fully sharp; making that the default for every deployment is next.
  • Scans as first-class citizens. Gaussian-splat captures from a phone already stream through the same pipeline; the next step is the same walk-through, review and video tooling for them that meshes already have.
  • In-editor publishing everywhere. The Blender button is verified end to end; Unity and Unreal are a smoke test away from the same. (Update, 4.0: the Unity and Unreal plug-ins have since been verified in the real editors — Unity 6000.6.5f1 and Unreal Engine 5.8.3 — and are no longer beta.)

If you want to try it yourself, the getting-started guide takes about five minutes, and the live examples run the real engine on this very docs site. If you only want the one-sentence version: Verse turns a heavy 3D file into a link that opens in seconds, in the browser — and we measure it to make sure.
